Barlings
BAR-lingz
n. (the Lincolnshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1154, whose abbot was hanged for the rising of 1536)
Old English, the people of Bar or Baerla; a settlement name in -ingas.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Barlings in Lincolnshire was founded in 1154 and refounded on its final site soon after. In October 1536 the Lincolnshire Rising broke out against the dissolution of the smaller monasteries and the religious changes behind it; Barlings canons joined the rebels, supplying men and horses, and the abbot Matthew Mackerell was taken, tried, and hanged at Tyburn in 1537. A single fragment of the church tower still stands in a field. This dictionary records Barlings because its abbot's end raises the hardest political question Scripture answers, and the answer is not a slogan in either direction. Civil authority is ordained and resisting it is treated gravely, “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1), “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2). Submission is for the Lord's sake, “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13). And yet when a command runs directly against God's, the apostles disobey openly and say why, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rebellion as open resistance to lawful authority; treason as the offense of attempting to overthrow the government; allegiance as the tie which binds a subject to the state; to submit as to yield to authority; and conscience as the internal judgment of right and wrong.

expand to see more

REBELLION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance; open resistance to lawful authority.

TREASON, n. In the United States, treason is confined to the actual levying of war against the state, or adhering to its enemies.

ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; the duty of fidelity to a king, government or state.

SUBMIT, v.t. To let down; to yield, resign or surrender to the power, will or authority of another.

CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.

Key Scripture

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Rom 13:2 — "Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation."

1Pe 2:13 — "Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;"

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Modern Corruption

Lincolnshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1154: its canons joined the rising of 1536 and its abbot was hanged at Tyburn.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture holds two things here that are usually separated for convenience. Paul, writing under Nero, grounds civil authority in God's own ordering and calls resistance to it resistance to God, “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2), and Peter makes the submission an act of worship rather than of prudence, “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13).

But the same apostles, ordered by a lawful council to stop preaching, refused outright and gave the ground, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The distinction is between a command that is unjust and a command that requires sin, and the second is the only warrant Scripture gives. Abbot Mackerell rode out against a king's commissioners over the fate of his house and his lands, which is a different matter from being ordered to deny Christ; the dictionary records his courage and does not call his cause the apostles'.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek exousia (G1849), authority; Greek tasso (G5021), to appoint; Greek antitassomai (G498), to set oneself against; Greek hupotasso (G5293), to submit; Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority.

expand to see more

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, as a thing ordained; “the powers that be are ordained of God”, Romans 13:1.

Greek antitassomai (G498) — to set oneself in array against; “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power”, Romans 13:2.

Greek diatage (G1296) — an ordinance, an arrangement; “resisteth the ordinance of God”, Romans 13:2.

Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to place oneself under; “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man”, 1 Peter 2:13.

Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; “We ought to obey God rather than men”, Acts 5:29.

Usage

"“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — written under Nero."

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — said to a lawful council."

"“Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13) — submission as worship, not prudence."
